source_note: Daily Compilation of Presidential Documents, a US Government work in the public domain.
sample: every third sentence of src.pipeline.segment.segment(), 0-indexed: [::3], 120 of 359
sample_note: Systematic rather than random so the set spans the whole speech and anyone can reproduce exactly which sentences were labelled.
rubric: check_worthy = the sentence asserts something about the world that could in principle be looked up and found true or false. NOT check-worthy: questions, imperatives, statements of intent or policy preference ('we should', 'I will keep pushing'), value judgements ('it's the right thing to do'), predictions, and rhetoric too vague to verify. A sentence counts as check-worthy if it embeds a verifiable claim even when its surface form is an imperative.
rubric_note: Labelled against this general definition and NOT against the heuristic's rules. In particular the heuristic's 'anchor' requirement (a name, number or date) is a limitation of the retrieval stack, not part of what makes a claim check-worthy -- so recall is expected to suffer where a real claim carries no anchor, and that gap is the thing worth measuring.
labeller: project author, single annotator, no second pass
limitation: The heuristic and these labels share an author, so this measures internal consistency of one person's judgement, not inter-annotator agreement. Treat it as a sanity check with known bias, not independent validation. A second annotator relabelling this same file is the fix.
